text: Fraud is the hard case of imbalanced classification. In this illustrative data, fewer than one transaction in a hundred is fraudulent. Accuracy is useless, investigators can only review so many alerts, and a model's value depends entirely on what it finds inside that budget.

Fifty thousand card transactions, and only three hundred thirty-four are fraud, a rate of zero point six seven percent. A model that says legitimate every time would be ninety-nine point three percent accurate and catch nothing. Stratifying the split keeps two hundred fifty-one fraud cases in training and eighty-three in test; eighty-three is small, so every estimate that follows is noisy.

Compare three candidates on PR-AUC, the area under the precision-recall curve, far more sensitive than ROC AUC when positives are scarce. Plain logistic regression scores point two three one. Adding class_weight equals balanced actually drops it to point one six seven. Gradient boosting with per-fold sample weights scores best, point two three seven.

Two lessons stand out: boosting barely beats logistic regression given the spread, and balanced weighting here hurt ranking quality instead of helping it. Weights move the operating point; they don't automatically make a better ranker. Test it, don't assume it.

Report it as a review budget. Investigators can check two percent of transactions, two hundred fifty alerts. Of those, forty-four are real fraud: a precision of seventeen point six percent, about twenty-seven times the base rate, and a recall of fifty-three percent. Reviewing two percent of transactions catches roughly half of all the fraud.

Here's the picture: precision-recall curves for all three candidates, with the base rate as a dashed line. The curve that sits furthest above that dashed line is adding the most value over random guessing, and with only eighty-three fraud cases in the test set, that gap could shift on another sample.

Stratify every split, measure weighting instead of assuming it helps, and report alerts, catches, and uncertainty together. Next: documenting a modeling project so someone else can trust and rebuild it.
